posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the explainability gap as the real blocker, position auditability as the missing layer between AI and trust
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense to me. It's not really an AI problem — it's a 'can I stand behind this number in a room full of regulators' problem, and most AI tools weren't built with that question in mind. The output gets smarter but the audit trail stays invisible. I wonder how many analytics teams are quietly in the same spot but haven't pulled the trigger yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the trust gap as the real problem, not the tooling
posts.draft_comment: The trust gap is the actual product nobody ships. Eighteen months on the dashboard, zero months on why your finance team believes the numbers — that's usually how it goes. In my experience the Excel exports aren't laziness, they're a signal that something in the data lineage or the definitions never got signed off properly. What did the finance team say when you asked them what it would take to actually trust it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: VP Ops sharing a 47→5 KPI story with a Director of Operations (ICP) engaging — validate the ruthless simplification, add the 'why dashboards stay bloated' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is almost never an analytics problem — it's a politics problem. Everyone wants their metric on the dashboard, so nothing gets cut, and eventually nobody opens it. The teams I see get this right usually had one person willing to be the villain and say 'that number doesn't change a decision, so it doesn't belong here.' How did you actually get internal buy-in on the cuts?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure thread — validate the 'who owns truth' pain point with a sharper framing around governance vs tooling
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem, it's a 'nobody decided who gets to define the numbers' problem before the licences were handed out. Tooling just makes the underlying mess move faster. I've seen teams spend more time arguing about which report is right than actually using the data. The real question isn't who owns the truth — it's who had that conversation before the rollout?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as security risk with CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust-chain insight that makes it stick
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here is the important bit — most teams are still treating hallucinated outputs as a QA problem when really it's a trust-chain problem. A wrong number in a report doesn't stop at the report. It travels into a decision, a budget, sometimes a board slide. Who in your org is actually responsible for catching it before it gets that far?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging on BI adoption failure in SMBs — validate the structural problem, add the 'built for builders not users' insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The £200k isn't even the worst part — it's the 18 months of internal goodwill that gets burned while everyone waits for the guy who built it to run their report. Most BI tools are genuinely brilliant at letting someone build dashboards. They're just not designed around the person who needs to ask a question at 8am before a client call. Wonder how many renewals get signed by the builder rather than the people who were supposed to benefit.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company naming the real problem (culture, not tooling) — validate the diagnosis but add the layer he's missing: culture problems often have a data governance root cause that tools can either worsen or help surface.
posts.draft_comment: The culture thing is real, but I'd push back slightly — three teams applying different filters isn't just a behaviour problem, it's a sign nobody agreed on what the numbers *mean* before they started using them. Most BI rollouts skip that conversation entirely and then wonder why trust breaks down. The CFO asking that question in a quarterly review is actually the best thing that could have happened. What did the three teams each think they were measuring?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure pattern — validate the shadow AI insight and add the missing layer: the problem isn't permission, it's that people don't know what questions are even worth asking their data.
posts.draft_comment: The shadow AI thing is the tell. When people prefer typing into a phone app over the tool you just licensed for them, it's not a compliance problem — it's a signal that the official tool doesn't feel like it understands their work. The 'nobody knows what to ask' problem is the one I keep seeing go unsolved. You can unlock every feature and it still won't fix that.
